newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean prosecutors to question president's son.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean prosecutors to question president's son.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors said on Sunday they would question a son of President Kim Young-sam, in connection with a loan scandal involving failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Prosecutors said they would question Hyun-chul, Kim's second son, sometime after he lodges a criminal libel complaint over allegations made by two opposition members of parliament.
Hyun-chul told reporters he had nothing to do with Hanbo's loans and has said he will file the libel suit on Monday with prosecutors handling the scandal.
"We will investigate the president's son," a prosecution official told Reuters.
The investigation would focus on the charge of libel against the opposition, but the prosecutor added that it would also consider the allegations made against Hyun-chul.
"They are like both faces of a coin," the official said.
The two lawmakers from the main opposition National Congress for New Politics alleged they had evidence Hyun-chul maintained links to Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate.
The party has accused him of playing a key role in brokering loans to Hanbo Steel, which went insolvent on January 23 after piling up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in debt.
The speculation was further fanned on Saturday by the discovery of more than 10,000 copies of a book written by Hyun-chul in a Hanbo Group warehouse in Seoul.

The opposition says Hyun-chul and Hanbo chairman Chung Bo-keun knew each other well. It said the books found in the warehouse demonstrated that Hanbo had been a sponsor of Hyun-chul, who helped the company expand rapidly in recent years.
National Congress spokesman Chung Dong-young said his party also planned to ask Hyun-chul to appear at a special parliamentary committee that would separately probe the Hanbo scandal.
"The revelation about the books alone is enough reason why Hyun-chul must appear at parlimentary hearings," he said.
The National Assembly agreed to reconvene on February 17 for a 30-day session to discuss the scandal and review a controversial new labour law.
On Friday, state prosecutors said a three-week investigation into the Hanbo case was winding down with a clutch of President Kim's closest political allies and top bankers in custody.
But opposition parties and newspaper editorials have said the prosecution had failed to ferret out "real power" in the scandal and demanded a fuller probe.
Prosecutors said they had been focusing on unearthing evidence to support charges against nine people arrested for their roles in the scandal in the past three days.
Hanbo Steel, with a net worth of just $300 million, wrung $5.8 billion from a pliant financial system to build a large-scale steel mill, which analysts said makes no economic sense.

Those being held are a former cabinet minister and three lawmakers from the ruling party -- two of them Kim's top loyalists -- one opposition member of parliament, two bankers, the founder of Hanbo Group and his former executive.

The scandal has tarnished Kim's "Mr Clean" image and confused the issue of who will succeed him as president. Kim cannot seek a second term in elections in December and his role as kingmaker is now in jeopardy, throwing the contest wide open.
Kim Woo-suk resigned as Home Affairs minister on Wednesday and was taken into custody the next day on bribery charges.

Detained with the minister were ruling New Korea Party stalwart Hwang Byung-tai, who helped engineer the president's rise to power, and Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung. Both politicians were also charged with bribery.
